title: Design Detectability and a Ceiling Effect in a Preregistered Verifier‑in‑the‑Loop NL→Config Evaluation
abstract: We report a preregistered paired confirmatory evaluation (N=200 paired multi‑device intents) that measured the marginal benefit of a bounded generate–validate–repair pipeline placing a formal verifier (Batfish) in‑the‑loop versus a single‑pass LLM generation for natural‑language→configuration translation. The preregistered design used a shared initial LLM candidate per intent that served as both the baseline and the guarded pipeline's starting candidate. In the confirmatory cohort the shared initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator in every paired episode: baseline_success_count = 200, guarded_success_count = 200, repair_attempts = 0/200, paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0 (artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 and the preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Because the shared‑candidate design required the guarded branch to change that single candidate to create discordant pairs, the preregistered primary paired test is uninformative in this run. We (1) present the deterministic validator decision rule used to assign verifier_pass, (2) report artifact‑grounded counts and representative diagnostics that substantiate the ceiling effect, (3) explain why McNemar/bootstrap inference is vacuous under zero discordant pairs and how that traces to the preregistered detectability tradeoff, and (4) provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future preregistered NetOps evaluations that would expose marginal verifier utility.

sections.introduction: Generative language models are being investigated as components of NetOps toolchains that translate operator intent into device configurations and automation workflows. A common operational proposal is to place a formal network verifier into an LLM‑centric generate–validate–repair loop so that verifier counterexamples drive constrained repairs before device execution [Batfish lessons]. Quantifying the marginal benefit of such guarded pipelines—relative to single‑pass LLM generation—matters for operational adoption because it informs tradeoffs among latency, complexity, and safety. We preregistered the study CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 to answer: To what extent does an iterative generate–validate–repair loop using a formal verifier (Batfish) reduce critical semantic errors in LLM‑generated multi‑device configurations when tested in an emulation‑grounded closed‑loop evaluation? The preregistration defined a confirmatory paired design (N=200 paired intents), a single shared initial generation per intent (shared_initial_candidate), at most one verifier‑guided repair iteration, and Batfish‑based semantic checks. The run completed as preregistered but produced a design‑induced ceiling effect: the shared initial candidate already satisfied the deterministic validator for every paired episode and therefore the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to apply repairs. This outcome renders the preregistered primary paired test uninformative for the question of marginal repair utility under alternative generation semantics. The present paper documents the artifact‑grounded evidence for that conclusion, explains the underlying detectability tradeoff introduced by shared‑candidate pairing, and provides concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for future preregistered NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM‑driven NetOps research spans intent translation, configuration synthesis, repair, and agentic orchestration [Intent translation studies; NetLLMBench; OpsEval]. Surveys and architecture proposals emphasize verifier integration as a mitigation for unsafe or hallucinated configurations [survey and proposals]. Benchmark and executable testbed efforts demonstrate closed‑loop evaluation of LLM agents and advocate verifier assistance for reachability and policy checks [NetConfArena; OpsEval]. Formal verification engines (Batfish, Header Space Analysis, SMT‑based tools) are established detectors of semantic misconfigurations and are commonly recommended as validators in LLM‑augmented pipelines [Batfish history; HSA/SMT literature]. Prior empirical work reports improvement in syntactic/executable correctness when verifiers are used, but designs, task banks, and model families differ and leave open the question of marginal repair utility under tightly preregistered contrasts. Our contribution complements those lines by providing a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment and by exposing a concrete experimental design failure mode—detectability collapse—driven by generation semantics choices.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The study preregistration (CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001) defined the primary estimand as paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and specified an exact two‑sided McNemar test (alpha=0.05) plus a 95% bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Sampling and stratification. Confirmatory N = 200 distinct multi‑device intents were stratified into topology clusters: (A) 2 devices: 80 intents; (B) 3–4 devices: 80 intents; (C) 5–8 devices: 40 intents. The deterministic task generator and random seed = 42 were preregistered and archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Model, budget, and generation semantics. The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json). The preregistration fixed generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate: one shared initial LLM candidate was produced per intent and presented verbatim to both baseline and guarded conditions. The guarded pipeline could apply up to one verifier‑guided repair (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This shared‑candidate decision intentionally reduced generation variance across paired units but required the guarded stage to modify that single candidate to create discordant outcomes. Validator design and pass rule. We implemented a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) whose archived validator_trace contains validation_before and validation_after records per candidate. The validator assigns verifier_pass only when validation_after.valid == true AND validation_after.violation_count == 0. Practically this enforces three checks in sequence: (1) parsing/normalization and canonicalization of commands, (2) task‑payload constraint checks (presence and ordering of required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state invariants), and (3) Batfish reachability/policy checks executed on the emulated topology; Batfish counterexamples are translated into violation codes. Execution environment. Experiments used containerized Mininet‑style emulation with FRRouting and VyOS images and Batfish as the formal verifier. Timeouts, retry policies, and missingness handling followed the preregistration. All raw model responses, provider traces, validator traces, and logs were archived in the execution and analysis bundles for machine verification (execution/, analysis/ artifact paths). Analysis plan. The preregistered primary test compared per‑intent paired binary semantic outcomes (baseline vs guarded) with McNemar; secondary analyses included subgroup descriptions by topology cluster and an iteration‑wise cumulative pass curve. Missingness and contamination handling were preregistered: exact‑hash duplicates were excluded from the confirmatory N; high n‑gram overlap was flagged for sensitivity analysis; technical failures follow the missingness_plan and were archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and artifact summary. The execution completed as preregistered: planned_episode_count = 400 (200 baseline + 200 guarded), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json; execution/model_configuration.json). Primary artifact‑grounded counts. The analysis artifacts record complete_pair_count = 200 with a paired contingency table n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Marginal success counts were baseline_success_count = 200 and guarded_success_count = 200 (analysis/condition_summary.csv). Statistical inference. With zero discordant pairs the preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI for the paired absolute success‑rate difference is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). These outputs are mathematical consequences of identical paired outcomes: bootstrap resampling reproduces zero paired differences and McNemar is vacuous without discordant pairs. Repair activity and shared_initial identity. Because generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate was used, a single shared initial LLM candidate was generated per intent and supplied to both baseline and guarded conditions. For every confirmatory pair the shared initial candidate was identical to both baseline and guarded raw responses (representative files: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt and execution/responses/task-000001-baseline.txt/guarded.txt). Each archived validator_trace shows validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 for the shared initial candidate; consequently repair_applied == false for 200/200 confirmatory episodes and repair_attempts = 0/200. Representative task diagnostics. The archived representative tasks (six exemplars in execution/representative_tasks/) summarize task difficulty statistics: changed_interface_count = {1,2,2,2,2,2} (mean = 1.83, median = 2), required_command_count = {4,2,6,4,3,6} (mean = 4.17, median = 4), dependency_rule_count commonly = 2, and difficulty labels span medium/hard/very_hard. These diagnostics show confirmatory intents required nontrivial multi‑step workflows despite the ceiling effect. Contamination and exclusions. The preregistered contamination filters flagged zero exact‑hash duplicates in the confirmatory N and no high n‑gram overlap flags; no confirmatory episodes were excluded (analysis/contamination_summary.csv; execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Diagnostic vignette (artifact‑grounded). A representative exemplar (pair-000001) illustrates the factual chain. The shared initial response (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt) and both condition responses are identical: "interface edge1 admin down
interface edge1 vlan 30
interface edge1 mtu 1600
interface edge1 admin up
". The corresponding validator_trace (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json) records validation_after.valid == true, violation_count == 0, and repair_applied == false. This single‑task trace exemplifies why repair could not change the paired outcome. Limits of inference from these results. The confirmatory run establishes only that, under the chosen generation semantics and model family, the shared initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator for every confirmatory intent. It does not permit generalization about the absolute utility of verifiers across models, temperatures, alternative generation semantics, adversarial tasks, or other emulation images; the preregistered design choice traded away sensitivity to marginal repair effects in favor of within‑pair generation control.
sections.discussion: Detectability tradeoff explained. Paired designs aim to control between‑intent variance by presenting closely matched or identical starting material to both conditions. When the shared_start candidate is identical across arms, the only path to discordance is an intervention‑driven change (here, a repair). If the shared candidate frequently satisfies the validator, the guarded pipeline has no opportunity to act and the paired contrast is blind to potential marginal repair utility that might appear under independent or more variable generation semantics. Formalizing the detectability collapse. Let S be the event that the shared candidate passes the validator. If P(S) ≈ 1, the probability of observing discordant pairs (n10 + n01 > 0) approaches zero regardless of repair effectiveness conditional on failing candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a baseline failure rate and a nontrivial discordant pair mass; those assumptions were not satisfied by the realized shared candidate distribution, causing empirical power collapse. Design alternatives to restore detectability. Based on archived artifacts and preregistered parameters, several artifact‑grounded alternatives would increase detection opportunity without inventing new runs: (A) independent per‑condition generation: produce separate LLM candidates for baseline and guarded arms per intent (increase across‑arm variance but permit the guarded stage to repair independent failures), (B) multiple independent draws per condition (k>1) and aggregate by best‑pass candidate, (C) sample multiple model families or temperatures to surface heterogeneous failure modes, (D) include adversarial/noisy intent strata targeted to stress ordering and reachability constraints, and (E) extend maximal repair iterations or allow verifier‑augmented retrieval for richer repair prompts. Each proposed alternative directly addresses the shared‑candidate detectability failure observed in the archived run. Trace‑centered evaluation metrics. The run demonstrates value in complementing final pass/fail outcomes with trace‑centered measures that can reveal potential repair utility even when final outcomes coincide: repair_attempts, repair_prompt traces, Batfish counterexample provenance, number and type of violation_codes, and repair_applied flags. Our artifact bundle contains these traces (execution/scoring/*.json and execution/provider_calls/*) and supports reproducible secondary analyses that focus on process evidence rather than only on final pass rates. Operational implications. For practitioners considering verifier‑in‑the‑loop deployments, the lesson is practical: if operational pipelines use a single authoritative initial candidate (for auditability or approval), a verifier that merely approves that candidate will rarely exercise repair logic; to realize repair gains, pipelines must either surface diverse candidate proposals or incorporate adversarial testing and active perturbation to expose plausible failures prior to repair. Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate choice and single model family (gpt‑5‑mini) limit within‑study sensitivity. Construct validity: deterministic validator rules map to a conservative notion of verifier_pass; alternative validators or more permissive normalization could alter pass rates. External validity: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only; no vendor diversity. Conclusion validity: zero discordant pairs eliminate the information needed for the preregistered McNemar test; bootstrap CI degeneracy reflects the observed determinism. These threats are supported by archived artifacts (analysis/missingness_summary.csv; execution/model_configuration.json).
sections.conclusion: This fully preregistered and archived paired evaluation exposes a concrete experimental design lesson for NetOps researchers: generation semantics are a design lever that trades variance control for detectability of verifier utility. In our confirmatory cohort (N=200 pairs) the shared initial candidate matched both baseline and guarded responses for every episode; no verifier repairs were applied (repair_attempts = 0/200) and the paired contingency was n11 = 200, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0, rendering McNemar/bootstrap inference vacuous (p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00]). The artifact bundle substantiates these facts and enables reproducible diagnostics, but does not permit broader generalization beyond the declared model, generation semantics, task generator, verifier, and emulation choices. We recommend that future preregistered NetOps evaluations (1) explicitly consider detectability when selecting generation semantics, (2) include trace‑centered metrics that reveal repair activity and provenance, and (3) use independent or multiple draws per condition (or multi‑model sampling) when the objective is to quantify marginal repair benefit. The archived evidence and traces we provide support reproducible post‑hoc inspection and should help the community design confirmatory NetOps experiments that avoid ceiling effects of the kind documented here.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory). The study was executed autonomously from a frozen initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Declared LLM: gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. Orchestration/adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 was frozen before execution (preregistration_sha256 = 163150627c4bd8d1e2520caeaa8ac0f4e0aa78876c16c3246e91596c632e49ec). Execution components: containerized Mininet‑style emulation using FRRouting and VyOS images; Batfish as the formal verifier; deterministic task generator; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scoring rule. The validator assigns verifier_pass when the archived validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 in the validator_trace; this combines parsing/normalization, required‑sequence and preserved‑state checks, and Batfish reachability/policy tests (see Methods and execution/scoring/*.json). The confirmatory run used a shared initial generation per intent for baseline and guarded conditions (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate), a preregistered design choice that intentionally controls generation variance and produced the observed detectability tradeoff. All experiment orchestration, model calls, verifications, emulation runs, scoring, logging, and analysis were performed autonomously per the preregistration; humans acted only as Research Director prior to the autonomy lock and to receive final outputs after autonomous completion. Execution completed without technical restarts affecting confirmatory pairs (completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). The artifact bundle includes archived raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts (refer to execution/ and analysis/ paths in the bundle) for machine verification.
limitations: Single model family: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; conclusions do not generalize across models or families.
Device and vendor scope: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only (no proprietary vendor images).
Synthetic deterministic task generator: tasks were deterministically generated and may not capture full operator ambiguity, legacy runbook phrasing, or adversarial intent distributions.
Emulator fidelity: containerized Mininet‑style emulation does not fully replicate hardware idiosyncrasies, timing, or race conditions of production devices.

Design detectability tradeoff: shared_initial_generation was chosen to control generation variance but reduces sensitivity to detect marginal repair benefits (a principal internal‑validity limitation).
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑pass outputs passed the validator for all confirmatory intents, producing a null marginal effect and limiting exploratory inference.

Contamination uncertainty: deterministic exact‑hash checks found zero matches in confirmatory N and n‑gram overlap detectors reported no high‑overlap flags, but undetected paraphrase overlap with model training data cannot be fully ruled out.
Security scenarios: prompt‑injection, retrieval poisoning, and adversarial telemetry perturbations were not evaluated and remain open threats for agentic NetOps systems.
